summary.text: A 63-year-old Caucasian female was thromboprophylaxed with warfarin for a pulmonary embolism history within the past 7 months, with a positive lupus anticoagulant blood test at the time of the embolism. Her past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, depression, CAD, arthritis, anxiety and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with a positive serotonin-release unfractionated heparin assay. She presented to the anticoagulation clinic with a subtherapeutic INR of 1.4 after missing one or possibly two doses of warfarin.

Table 2 lists platelets of 260 on 21 January 2016 at 11:55 and 109 (L) at 23:00, with heparin initiation at 13:51 during hospital admission. On 4 February 2016 platelets were 150, and heparin initiation had a bolus at 19:27 and infusion at 20:51. On 6 February 2016 platelets were 55 (L); HIT was suspected, heparin discontinued and labs ordered, and at 13:39 SRA UF (Porcine) was Positive (A), SRA UF HEP LOW DOSE 100 % and PF4 Ab, IgG 2.790 (H).

Her daily medication list before outpatient fondaparinux use comprised aspirin 81 mg, nitroglycerin 0.4 mg as needed, escitalopram 10 mg, pantoprazole 40 mg, furosemide 20 mg, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, metformin XR 750 mg, metoprolol succinate 50 mg and warfarin 1 mg and 3 mg tablets; platelets were 194 on 19 September 2016. She was instructed to increase her warfarin dose and was given fondaparinux 7.5 mg subcutaneously once daily.

She was instructed to have a complete blood count on day 3 and 5 of fondaparinux therapy, and an INR recheck was scheduled after the fifth day. Platelets were 167 on 4 October 2016, 3 days post-fondaparinux outpatient exposure, and the INR was 2.6 (within goal range) after five doses. She tolerated fondaparinux without bleeding, thromboembolic event or thrombocytopenia, and without a significant reduction in platelets.

article_limitations: Single case; the article has no figures, supplements or videos, and Tables 2 and 3 are text tables.
Table 2 value cells print no unit: the platelet and PF4 units are read from the row Reference Range cell and the SRA UF HEP LOW DOSE unit from its "Units: %" cell, all kept literal.
Table 2 comment cells print clock times without a date: comment-derived items take only the column date and keep the clock time in the regimen text; the lab draw clock times are not applied to them.
The fondaparinux start date and the clinic visit date are not stated; the day 3 and 5 blood counts are instructions, and no day 5 count is reported.
The number of missed warfarin doses is "one or possibly two" and no exact count is recorded.

Two Table 2 comments mention hospital admission and heparin initiation appears on two dates; admission dates, number and reason are not stated and were not inferred or merged, and the admission context is kept in evidence and event descriptions rather than as separate care-episode facts.
Table 2 comments are aligned to the date columns by cell position (two comment positions are blank); the platelet row and the comment row have the same number of cells as the header row.

Table 3 is a medication list headed "Current Daily Medications" and captioned as prior to outpatient fondaparinux use: the items are recorded as administered at that list time (before the fondaparinux use) with temporality unknown, since the source does not place them at the latest described time.
No allergy statement is made; the history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is recorded once, as a condition.
Literature review text, guideline comparisons, hypothetical drug costs and Table 1 adverse-effect rates are not patient facts and were not recorded.
The case text uses an identifying pseudonym for the patient; it is not stored in any authored field and is avoided in quotes where possible.
